source: Turney (2006) Similarity of Semantic Relations
finding: Latent Relational Analysis (LRA) beat the earlier fixed-pattern vector space model (VSM) on 374 SAT analogy questions and matched average high-school test takers.
numbers: LRA recall 56.1% (210/374 right), precision 56.8%, 95% CI for recall 51.0-61.2. VSM on AltaVista 47.1% (CI 42.2-52.5). VSM on the same local corpus as LRA 38.5% (CI 33.5-43.6). Human average about 57%. Chance 20%.
limits: Human 57% is an estimate from the verbal SAT, not measured on these 374 items. LRA vs human not significant; LRA vs both VSM variants significant (Fisher exact, 95%).
agent_relevance: Relational similarity from corpus counts reaches human-average on word analogies. It is a baseline to beat, not a reasoner.

source: Turney (2006) Similarity of Semantic Relations
finding: Ablations show which parts of LRA matter. Synonym substitution and learned patterns carry the gain. The SVD smoothing step did not show a significant gain on this small set.
numbers: No SVD: drop not significant. No synonyms: recall 56.1% to 49.5%, skipped questions 4 to 22. LRA without SVD and without synonyms still beats VSM-WMTS significantly, so 4,000 learned patterns (8,000 dims) beat the fixed 64 joining terms (128 dims).
limits: Matrix was 8,000 columns by 17,232 rows, small next to LSA matrices; author says the SVD benefit likely needs more pairs. Not shown.
agent_relevance: Sparse-data repair (swap in near words) beat pure smoothing. When an exact relation pair is rare, retry with near synonyms of each side.

source: Turney (2006) Similarity of Semantic Relations
finding: Cost and data sensitivity: LRA took almost nine days of compute for 374 questions; the older VSM on AltaVista took 17 days (with 5 second query delays) and VSM on the local corpus took one day.
numbers: LRA about 9 days; VSM-AV 17 days; VSM-WMTS 1 day. LRA corpus about 5x10^10 words; AltaVista about 5x10^11 words. VSM-WMTS skipped 34 questions versus 5 for VSM-AV.
limits: 2006 hardware (2.4 GHz Xeons). The corpus was a web-crawl passage index, not Wikipedia.
agent_relevance: Cheap similarity today means embeddings or a small model call; LRA-style corpus counting is not cheap.

source: Turney (2006) Similarity of Semantic Relations
finding: Item subset and parameter checks. Official-test items were easier for LRA than the added items, and results moved only a few points across parameter settings.
numbers: 190 items from ten official SAT tests: LRA 61.1%; other 184 items: 51.1%. Parameter sweep kept recall about 53.5 to 56.1, best at num_sim 10, k 300, 4000 patterns.
limits: Parameters tuned on the same 374 items, so 56.1 is probably slightly optimistic.
agent_relevance: Report on held-out items; do not tune the scaffold on the test set.

source: Turney (2006) Similarity of Semantic Relations
finding: The same vectors classify noun-modifier relations, where LRA again beat VSM.
numbers: 30-class: LRA recall 41.0%, precision 39.8%; VSM recall 27.8%. 5-class: LRA recall 55.9%, precision 58.0%; VSM 45.7%. 600 noun-modifier pairs, leave-one-out nearest neighbour.
limits: One dataset of 600 pairs; chance 3.3% and 20%.
agent_relevance: Relation labels from corpus patterns work modestly; later fine-tuned encoders beat this.

source: Turney and Littman (2005) Corpus-based learning of analogies and semantic relations
finding: The original VSM for analogies: count how often two words appear with each of 64 joining terms in 128 phrases, then take the cosine of two pair vectors.
numbers: SAT 374 items: 176 right, 193 wrong, 5 skipped; precision 47.7%, recall 47.1%, F 47.4%. Human 57%, chance 20%. Noun-modifier: F 26.5% (30 classes, chance 3.3%) and 43.2% (5 classes, chance 20%).
limits: Used AltaVista hit counts, which cannot be reproduced today.
agent_relevance: Founding cheap-similarity result: vector of pattern counts, then cosine.

source: Turney (2005) Measuring semantic similarity by Latent Relational Analysis (IJCAI)
finding: First LRA report: 56.4% on the SAT items (210 of 374) against 47.3% for VSM-AV and 40.3% for VSM on the local corpus.
numbers: LRA 56.4% (210/374); VSM-AV 47.3%; VSM-WMTS 40.3%. Noun-modifier: LRA precision 39.8% and recall 41.0% (30 classes), 58.0% and 55.9% (5 classes); VSM recall 27.8% and 45.7%.
limits: Conference version. The journal paper reports 56.1% recall because of how skipped items are scored.
agent_relevance: The 56.4 figure is the one later LLM papers cite as the LRA baseline.

source: Turney, Littman, Bigham, Shnayder (2003) Combining independent modules to solve multiple-choice synonym and analogy problems
finding: An ensemble of 13 modules on SAT analogies; the phrase-vector (VSM) module was the biggest contributor.
numbers: SAT ensemble 45.0% with the phrase-vector module versus 37.0% without it (logarithmic rule). TOEFL synonyms: PMI-IR alone 69.0%, LSA alone 43.8%, thesaurus alone 69.6%, mixture 80.2%, logarithmic 82.0%. Average applicant TOEFL 64.5%.
limits: The analogy test here was a smaller set of 100 items; 2003 modules were weak.
agent_relevance: Combining weak views with calibrated probabilities beat any single view; a pattern for ensembling checks.

source: Turney (2008) A uniform approach to analogies, synonyms, antonyms, and associations (PairClass)
finding: PairClass casts four word-pair tasks as supervised classification over corpus-pattern features. Competitive but below the best task-specific systems.
numbers: SAT 52.1% (LRA 56.1%, human about 57%). TOEFL 76.2% (best known 97.5%, applicants 64.5%). Synonym-antonym (136 ESL questions) 75.0% against majority 65.4%. Similar/associated/both, 144 pairs, ten-fold CV: 77.1% against 33.3%.
limits: Needs labelled training pairs; small test sets.
agent_relevance: One relation-pair representation can serve several lexical judgments; supports reusing a single similarity routine.

source: Mikolov et al. (2013) Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space
finding: Neural embeddings solved analogies by vector offset (king - man + woman near queen) at far lower cost than corpus-count methods.
numbers: Test set: 8,869 semantic and 10,675 syntactic questions (19,544 total). Only the exact nearest word counts. Reported totals range from about 36% to about 56% depending on model, dimension and training words.
limits: Synonyms count as errors. Test is dominated by capitals and morphology.
agent_relevance: The cheap 2013 alternative to LRA. It looks strong only on easy relation types (see later critiques).

source: Levy and Goldberg (2014) Linguistic regularities in sparse and explicit word representations
finding: The analogy ability is not special to neural embeddings. Sparse explicit count vectors recover it too when the scoring rule is fixed (multiplicative 3CosMul instead of additive 3CosAdd).
numbers: 3CosAdd: embedding MSR 53.98%, Google 62.70%; explicit 29.04% and 45.05%. 3CosMul: embedding 59.09% and 66.72%; explicit 56.83% and 68.24%. Google set 19,544 questions. Per-category spread is large (capital-common-countries 90.51% explicit vs 99.41% embedding; currency 14.55% vs 10.53%).
limits: Single corpus; explicit vectors have very high dimension.
agent_relevance: Count-based methods (LRA's heirs) match neural vectors if scored well; the scoring rule matters as much as the vectors.

source: Linzen (2016) Issues in evaluating semantic spaces using word analogies
finding: Much of the offset-method success comes from the target word simply being near the query word. Baselines that ignore the offset recover a large part of the score.
numbers: Overall ADD accuracy .53 (window 2), .60 (window 5), .58 (window 10). IGNORE-A baseline .41, .29, .26; ONLY-B baseline .42, .36, .33. Without excluding input words, the nearest neighbour was b in 93% of cases. Reversing the direction cut accuracy by 0.11 on average. ADD by category ranges .13 to .90; currencies .12.
limits: Skip-gram spaces on ukWaC plus Wikipedia only.
agent_relevance: If an agent uses vector arithmetic for relations, compare to a baseline that ignores the offset, and exclude the input words.

source: Gladkova, Drozd, Matsuoka (2016) Analogy-based detection of morphological and semantic relations with word embeddings (BATS)
finding: BATS, a larger and balanced test, showed the Google-set scores were flattering.
numbers: BATS: 99,200 questions in 40 categories. GloVe falls from 80.4% on the Google set to 28.5% on BATS. Google accuracy varied between 10.53% and 99.41% by category. SVD model 49.9% on Google (Levy et al. reported 52.6%). One embedding reached only 15.9% on BATS.
limits: Authors' own runs; 2016 vectors.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks with easy morphology inflate the apparent power of vector relational similarity.

source: Drozd, Gladkova, Matsuoka (2016) Word embeddings, analogies, and machine learning: beyond king - man + woman
finding: A supervised set-based method (LRCos) beats offset arithmetic, with gains up to 30 points on some embeddings and relations.
numbers: On the Google set, singular-plural gets 70% by returning the nearest neighbour of b. LRCos on BATS reaches only 47.7% average. SVD1000 on Google: 3CosAdd 58.1% vs LRCos 74.6%. GloVe and Skip-Gram gain less because the simple average 3CosAvg works nearly as well.
limits: LRCos needs several example pairs per relation.
agent_relevance: Several examples of a relation beat one example pair. Few-shot exemplars help even in vector space.

source: Rogers, Drozd, Li (2017) The (too many) problems of analogical reasoning with word vectors
finding: Offset arithmetic depends on how close the vectors already are, not on a clean relation. Accuracy tracks vector similarity.
numbers: Nearest neighbour of b alone gives about 70% on Google singular-plural; 3CosAdd adds only about 10 points. Best GloVe model under 30% on BATS. About 40% of successful questions had b within 10 neighbours of the target; over 40% of low-accuracy questions were over 90 neighbours away. Without excluding query words, accuracy fell to zero in 9 of 15 Google categories (citing Linzen 2016).
limits: Mainly GloVe and Word2vec on BATS.
agent_relevance: Treat embedding similarity as topical closeness unless the relation is tested separately.

source: Chen, Peterson, Griffiths (2017) Evaluating vector-space models of analogy
finding: Human relational-similarity ratings were compared with word2vec and GloVe parallelogram predictions. Fit varied by relation, and vector geometry breaks human patterns.
numbers: SemEval-2012 Task 2 data. Experiment 1: 823 recruited, 158 excluded; mean human rating 5.01 within-subtype, 4.02 between-subtype, 2.70 between-type. Cosine fails on SIMILAR, CONTRAST and NON-ATTRIBUTE relations. Experiment 2 (1,102 recruited, 99 excluded): 77 comparisons differed by presentation order, 25 expected by chance (p < .001); angry:smile vs exhausted:run rated 4.76 one way and 2.36 the other. Experiment 3 triads: type 1-2 and 2-3 ratings 5.44 and 5.43, type 1-3 only 2.99, violating the triangle inequality that vector distance obeys; model predictions did not differ by type (word2vec p = .31, GloVe p = .79).
limits: Mechanical Turk samples; 300-d vectors from Google News and GloVe.
agent_relevance: Human relations are asymmetric and not transitive; one cosine cannot copy that. Do not assume relational similarity is symmetric.

source: Ethayarajh, Duvenaud, Hirst (2019) Towards understanding linear word analogies
finding: A theory of why offset analogies work for SGNS and GloVe vectors: they hold when word pairs are frequent enough that noise is small.
numbers: Countries and capitals (median pair frequency 3,436.5 in Wikipedia) solved with 95.4% accuracy; countries and currencies (median frequency 19) only 9.2%. Correlation between csPMI and the offset-error term Pearson r > 0.50.
limits: Theory plus Wikipedia embeddings; rare relations fail.
agent_relevance: Predicts when cheap relation vectors fail: rare pairs. Add a check on how common a relation is.

source: Allen and Hospedales (2019) Analogies explained: towards understanding word embeddings
finding: A second theory: a paraphrase-based explanation that links offsets to analogies with explicit error terms.
numbers: Theory paper; abstract only.
limits: Not read in full.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that vector analogies are an approximate side effect, not designed relational reasoning.

source: Nissim, van Noord, van der Goot (2020) Fair is better than sensational: man is to doctor as woman is to doctor
finding: Offset analogies as a bias probe are distorted by the rule that forbids returning an input word.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: I read the opening pages only, not the experimental section.
agent_relevance: Another warning that the all-terms-different constraint shapes results.

source: Ushio, Espinosa-Anke, Schockaert, Camacho-Collados (2021) BERT is to NLP what AlexNet is to CV: can pre-trained language models identify analogies?
finding: Zero-shot language-model scoring of analogy candidates. LRA still led on SAT among untuned unsupervised systems. BERT did not beat word embeddings.
numbers: Full SAT (374): LRA 56.4; GPT-3 zero-shot 53.7, few-shot 65.2 (uses training examples); FastText 49.7; GloVe 48.9; word2vec 42.8; PMI 23.3; random 20.0. Default prompts: BERT 32.6, GPT-2 41.4, RoBERTa 49.6. Tuned on the data: BERT 42.8, GPT-2 57.8, RoBERTa 55.8. Google: FastText 96.6; BATS: GPT-2 tuned 81.2 vs FastText 72.0.
limits: Tuned figures choose hyperparameters on the test data, so they are upper bounds. Very sensitive to prompt and two score parameters.
agent_relevance: Prompt and scoring choices move analogy accuracy by 15 to 25 points. An agent needs a fixed, pre-registered scoring rule.

source: Ushio, Camacho-Collados, Schockaert (2021) Distilling relation embeddings from pre-trained language models (RelBERT)
finding: Fine-tuning a masked LM on SemEval-2012 relation data gave relation vectors that beat LRA and few-shot GPT-3 on SAT with no SAT training.
numbers: RelBERT with manual prompt: SAT full 69.5 (test part 70.6), U2 66.2, U4 65.3, Google 92.4, BATS 78.8. AutoPrompt 61.0 SAT; P-tuning 54.0. Baselines: LRA 56.4, SuperSim 54.8, GPT-3 zero 53.7, GPT-3 few 65.2, FastText 49.7, GloVe 48.9. A journal version is said to report 73% on SAT (search snippet only, not read).
limits: Trained on SemEval-2012 relations, which overlap some analogy relations. Google set is biased toward word similarity.
agent_relevance: A small trained relation encoder gives cheap relational similarity better than raw LLM prompting.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 passed the estimated average SAT level on 374 word analogies and matched people on other verbal-analogy sets.
numbers: SAT 374 items scored by log-probability of each of five C:D choices; GPT-3 above the estimated high-school average (exact figure only in a figure). Verbal sets: UCLA VAT (human N=57), Sternberg and Nigro (N=20), Jones et al. (N=241); GPT-3 numerically weaker than people on Jones et al.
limits: Training-set contamination not excluded for SAT items (public since 2003). Later work found brittleness.
agent_relevance: Word-pair analogy is no longer a hard test for LLMs; do not use it to prove reasoning.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: A counterfactual replication of Webb et al. GPT models fell sharply on altered letter-string problems while people stayed high. The authors skipped word-pair analogies because LLMs find them easy, probably through learned embeddings.
numbers: Letter-string variants: GPT accuracy dropped sharply, human accuracy stayed high on two variant types. Digit matrices: drop on one of two variants. Story analogies: answer-order effects and paraphrase sensitivity in GPT, not in humans.
limits: Tests three of Webb's four domains; word-pair analogies not retested.
agent_relevance: Success on familiar analogy formats may be retrieval. Check the agent on altered, unseen forms.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) Analogical structure abduction (SCAR) with word-analogy test
finding: Chat models score near or above people on word-analogy sets, but word-analogy accuracy does not track structure-mapping accuracy.
numbers: Word analogy accuracy % (E-KAR/BATS/U2/U4/Google/SAT): embedding baseline 30.5/30.2/34.7/33.6/50.4/36.7; ChatGPT zero-shot 53.1/92.4/76.3/71.3/98.8/74.8; ChatGPT 1-shot SAT 83.7; InstructGPT-002 zero-shot SAT 37.4; human 77.8/84.9/87.5/66.7/99.4/57.0. Relational structure identification on E-KAR: ChatGPT 71.7 (0-shot), human 86.4. SCAR (400 science analogies, 13 fields): GPT-4 system accuracy about 65 to 69 across prompt types.
limits: GPT-4 rows unreadable in my text extract; human numbers copied by the authors from original papers.
agent_relevance: Word-pair accuracy is a weak proxy for mapping ability. Test mapping, not only A:B::C:D.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2024) KnowledgePrompts: proportional analogies via knowledge-enhanced prompting
finding: On a new 15K multiple-choice proportional-analogy set, the best of nine models reached only 55%. Targeted knowledge helped; bulk structured knowledge hurt.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo best, exact match 55.25% with targeted knowledge; zero-shot 45.7%; structured knowledge 38.29% (random) and 38.79% (semantic). Single-source knowledge averaged over all nine models: Wikidata 14.57%, WordNet 14.41%, ConceptNet 14.34%. 19.96% of questions were answered correctly under all three prompt types.
limits: Exact-match scoring; knowledge-prompt tests used 20% of the set.
agent_relevance: Targeted facts help; bulk retrieved knowledge hurts. Keep retrieved context short and specific.

source: Ushio et al. (2021) artefact check: masking head or tail of candidate answers
finding: Items hard for people are hard for models; masking half of a candidate pair leaves much of the score intact.
numbers: RoBERTa (smPPL) full vs masked head/tail: SAT 53.4 vs 38.6/35.6; U2 58.3 vs 37.7/37.3; Google 93.6 vs 60.6/55.8. Hard items are abstract (witness:testimony :: generator:electricity) or use rare words.
limits: Masking is a diagnostic; numbers are the authors' runs and the table layout in my extract was partly garbled.
agent_relevance: LLM relation scoring still works with half the answer hidden, so artefact checks are needed.
